SEO, AEO and GEO Services for Restaurants and Hospitality

Hospitality is the most decision-compressed industry I work in. A diner picks a table in under two minutes, usually one-handed, usually while already moving. A traveller books a room after comparing four options in a single sitting. Neither of them reads a homepage. They read a map result, a rating, an opening-hours line and, increasingly, a paragraph an AI assistant wrote about you.

That means the winning work happens before anyone reaches your website. It happens in the local pack, in structured data, in review signals and in whether a language model can state your cuisine, price range and opening hours without guessing.

Local search decides who gets the booking

Most restaurant discovery ends in the map pack. Three results, ranked on relevance, distance and prominence, with an Open now label doing more persuasive work than any tagline you will ever write. If your hours are wrong on a public holiday, you are not third — you are invisible for that query.

The unglamorous work carries this: a complete and actively maintained Google Business Profile, categories that match how people actually search, service attributes filled in, real photography rather than stock, and name, address and phone details identical everywhere they appear. Conflicting details across directories and aggregators are the single most common reason a well-reviewed restaurant underperforms in maps.

Your menu is data, not decoration

A menu published as a PDF or a flat image is invisible to every system that matters. It cannot be parsed, cannot be quoted, and cannot answer a constrained question like “vegan mains under £15 near me”.

Marked up properly, the same menu becomes an answer. Dish names, prices, cuisine, and dietary attributes such as halal, vegan and gluten-free stop being marketing copy and start being retrievable facts. Combined with Restaurant, Menu and OpeningHoursSpecification schema, that data is what an assistant repeats back to a hungry buyer. Anything you leave unmarked is left to inference, and inference favours whoever documented themselves better.

Reviews are the ranking signal you cannot write yourself

Rating and review volume feed both map rankings and the trust layer that generative engines lean on. What matters is not a one-off push to hit a number, but velocity and recency — a steady flow of recent, specific reviews beats a large pile of old ones.

I set up the asking mechanics so requests land at the moment the guest is happiest, then make sure responses are handled properly. Replying to criticism in public, calmly and specifically, converts better than any five-star average, because prospective guests read how you handle problems.

Multi-location groups and franchises

Groups fail differently from independents. Their problem is rarely visibility for the brand name and almost always cannibalisation between locations, thin duplicated location pages, and profiles managed inconsistently by individual venues.

The fix is architectural: one genuinely distinct page per location with real local content, clean internal linking from a parent hub, consistent naming across every profile, and location-level tracking so you can see which venues are actually pulling demand. This is the same structural discipline covered in my local SEO services, applied at group scale.

Hotels and hospitality: a longer, researched decision

Hotels behave differently from restaurants. The consideration window is longer, the queries are more specific — amenities, proximity to a venue, cancellation terms, family suitability — and third-party platforms occupy much of the results page.

The play is to answer those specific questions on your own pages, in extractable form, so you get quoted directly rather than only through an aggregator that charges commission on the booking. Amenity lists, policy clarity and genuine local guides earn that position.

Being the answer, not just the listing

Answer Engine Optimisation and Generative Engine Optimisation matter more in hospitality than in almost any other vertical, because the queries are naturally conversational. People ask assistants for a quiet restaurant for six on a Friday, or a hotel near a specific venue with late check-out. Those are constraint-filtering questions, and only machine-readable operators qualify for consideration.

My approach here mirrors the method in my AEO and GEO services: make the facts explicit, keep them consistent everywhere, and give independent sources something accurate to corroborate.

What an engagement actually involves

I start by auditing what a search engine and an assistant can currently establish about you — which is often less than owners expect. From there the sequence is access and accuracy first, then structure, then the reputation work that compounds. Technical health underpins all of it; if your pages are slow on a phone on mobile data, nothing else compensates, which is why technical SEO is never optional.

If you want to know what is currently holding your venue back, a free SEO audit is the fastest way to find out.

tabs.tab_title: How is SaaS SEO different from regular SEO?
tabs.tab_content: The intent structure differs. Software buyers search categories, comparisons and alternatives rather than your brand, so coverage of decision-stage queries matters more than publishing volume. The technical layer also matters more, because JavaScript-heavy apps and documentation platforms frequently block crawlers by default.

tabs.tab_title: Are comparison and “alternatives” pages worth building?
tabs.tab_content: They are usually the highest-converting organic pages a software company owns, because the buyer is at the end of the decision. They only work if they are honest and specific — a comparison that never concedes a point reads as marketing and gets ignored by both readers and models.

Frequently more than the marketing site. Docs attract links, answer long-tail technical queries and demonstrate genuine depth. If they are crawlable and structured they compound; if they sit behind JavaScript or a blocked subdomain they contribute nothing.

SEO, AEO and GEO Services for SaaS and Technology Companies

SaaS buyers do not search the way marketing teams assume. They rarely start with your brand name, and they almost never start with the feature you are proudest of. They start with a problem, then a category, then a shortlist — and by the time your name enters the process, most of the filtering has already happened somewhere you do not control.

That is why product-led SEO for software is less about publishing volume and more about owning the specific queries that decide a shortlist, then making sure an assistant can summarise your product accurately when asked.

The queries that actually decide the deal

Bottom-of-funnel intent in SaaS lives outside your brand. It looks like best [category] software, [competitor] alternatives, [you] vs [competitor], [category] for [role or industry], pricing questions and integration questions.

Each of those needs its own page with its own angle. A single features page cannot serve six different intents, and trying to make it do so is the most common reason technically strong products stay invisible. Comparison and alternative pages in particular feel uncomfortable to write because they name competitors — which is precisely why they convert and why they get cited.

Page architecture that scales without turning into sprawl

The architecture I build for software companies runs on four families: feature pages covering what the product does, use-case pages covering who it is for, integration pages covering what it connects to, and comparison pages covering why you over the alternatives.

Each family targets a different stage of the decision, and each adds entities that strengthen the others. Done properly this compounds; done carelessly it becomes hundreds of thin, templated pages that dilute the site. The dividing line is whether each page answers a question a real buyer asked, in language they used.

Documentation and changelogs are search assets

Most technology companies treat docs as a support cost. In practice, documentation is often the most linked, most cited and most specific content the company owns — developers search error messages, API methods and configuration questions constantly.

If your docs sit behind JavaScript, on a subdomain nobody links to, or in a tool that blocks crawlers, you are discarding your strongest technical authority signal. Making them crawlable, well-structured and internally linked is usually one of the highest-return technical fixes available, and it sits squarely inside technical SEO.

Third-party platforms decide part of your visibility

For software, review platforms and roundups occupy a large share of the results your buyers see. G2, Capterra, industry roundups and community threads frequently outrank vendor sites for category queries, and they are heavily used as sources by generative engines because they read as independent consensus.

You cannot rank a listing you do not own, but you can influence it: keep your category placement and product descriptions accurate, maintain review flow, and make sure the facts on those profiles match your own site exactly. Contradictions between your pricing page and your G2 profile are a trust problem before they are a ranking problem.

Getting recommended inside AI answers

Software evaluation is one of the fastest-moving categories for AI-assisted research. Buyers ask assistants to compare tools, summarise pricing models and recommend options for a stated constraint — team size, budget, compliance requirement, existing stack.

Being included in those answers depends on the same discipline as AEO and GEO anywhere else: state facts explicitly rather than implying them, structure pages so passages can be extracted cleanly, mark up SoftwareApplication and offer data, and ensure independent sources corroborate what you claim. Vague positioning language is invisible to a retrieval system.

Measuring what matters in SaaS

Sessions are a poor proxy for a business that sells subscriptions. I report on qualified signups and trials from organic, assisted conversions across the longer research path, and share of visibility on the specific comparison and category queries that precede a purchase.

I also run a fixed panel of buying prompts through the major assistants each month and log whether the product is mentioned and how it is described. When a model gets your pricing model or integration list wrong, that is a content gap you can fix — and it is usually costing you deals silently.

Where I would start

Almost always with coverage and structure rather than volume. I map the category, find which decision-stage queries have no page behind them, fix the technical issues blocking crawl and render, then build the missing pages in order of commercial value. Semantic SEO holds it together, keeping the whole site legible as one coherent subject rather than a pile of feature copy.
